# Bond ladder

Short gilt ladder in the general account at AJ Bell, set up Aug 2024 for one reason: low-coupon gilts are free of capital gains tax, and most of the return on them is the pull to par, not the coupon. For a higher-rate taxpayer that beats a savings account.

## The rungs

| Gilt | Code | Coupon | Matures | Bought | Price | Nominal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TN25 | 0 1/4% Treasury 2025 | 0.25% | 31 Jan 2025 | 12 Aug 2024 | 98.21 | £5,000 |
| T26 | 0 1/8% Treasury 2026 | 0.125% | 30 Jan 2026 | 12 Aug 2024 | 95.06 | £6,000 |
| TG27 | 0 1/8% Treasury 2027 | 0.125% | 31 Jan 2027 | 12 Aug 2024 | 91.47 | £6,000 |

Each rung is lined up with a January, so the money comes back just before the 31 January tax payment. See [[Tax deadline calendar]].

## How the maths works

TN25: paid £4,910.50 + £9.95 dealing for £5,000 back in under 6 months. The £89.50 gain is CGT-exempt; only the tiny coupon (£6.25) is income. Gross-equivalent yield for me at 40% came out at about 5.9%, versus the 4.1% on the Chase saver.

## January 2025: first rung matured

- £5,000 landed at AJ Bell on 31 Jan 2025
- Paid HMRC the balancing payment the same day from the Starling tax space. The gilt money then refilled the tax space.
- Decision: roll it into a new rung, TG28 (0 1/8% 2028)? Bought £5,000 nominal at 88.93 on 3 Feb 2025.

## Things to remember

- Clean vs dirty price. The dirty price includes accrued interest and that's what you pay. Tiny here but it confuses the contract note
- Do NOT hold these in the ISA. The CGT advantage is pointless inside a wrapper, and ISA room goes to [[Index funds]]
- Coupons are taxable even though small. They go on the return in the interest box
- Longer-term question for retirement is in [[Pension consolidation]]
